subject: Cooking
title: Tea and Independence: India's Swadeshi Movement
description: Learn Tea and Independence: India's Swadeshi Movement in one minute.

hook.text: British-owned Indian tea plantations were symbols of colonial extraction.

buildup.text: The Swadeshi movement (1905) urged Indians to reject British goods — including tea from British-owned estates.

discovery.text: Indian entrepreneurs started indigenous tea brands — proving India could control its own tea industry.

twist.text: After independence in 1947, India nationalized many British tea estates — but working conditions remained poor.

climax.text: Today, India is the world's second-largest tea producer — and its workers still earn as little as $2/day.

punchline.text: India won its tea industry back. Its workers are still waiting for their share.

quiz.question: What was the Swadeshi movement's stance on British tea?
options: Boycotted British-owned tea as a revolutionary act

details.summary: During India's independence struggle, the Swadeshi movement urged citizens to boycott British goods including imported tea. Indian-grown tea became a symbol of self-sufficiency.
details.whyItMatters: Tea went from colonial tool to independence symbol in India. The Swadeshi tea movement shows how food consumption becomes political action when a nation fights for sovereignty.
takeaways: Swadeshi movement promoted Indian-grown tea over British imports
Tea consumption became a symbol of self-reliance during independence
India now consumes over 80 percent of its own tea production

faq.question: How did the Swadeshi movement change India's tea culture?
faq.answer: The movement reframed tea from colonial product to patriotic drink when consumed domestically grown. After independence, government campaigns promoted tea drinking across India. The Indian Tea Board marketed chai to workers and communities.

faq.question: Why was tea politically significant during Indian independence?
faq.answer: British-owned plantations made tea visible as colonial exploitation — Indian land, Indian labor, British profit. Boycotting British tea and choosing Indian brands was a personal act of resistance accessible to everyone.
